The last proposition thus completes an answer for how, given $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ with $x_i\in U[0,1]$ for $1\leq i\leq n$ and $A=\kappa(X,X)$, we may design a framework for obtaining a matrix $B$ such that Corollary~\ref{cor:momentmatching} applies in expectation.
In particular, after fixing $k$, our framework provides bounds in expectation on the $k$ spectrum quantiles of the kernel matrix $A$.
suppose we have $\mathrm{tr}\left(B^r/k\right)=\mathrm{tr}\left(A^r/n\right)$ for $1\leq r\leq k$.

While we do not know of a way of matching these expected traces exactly
In general, as we see in \cite{jinmusco}, approximate moment matching for a guarantee of pointwise closeness of two cumulative distribution functions may require prohibitively close tolerances.

issues.failure_explanation: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion assert that the framework provides proved bounds on the eigenvalue quantiles of A. The only sandwich theorem, Corollary cor:momentmatching, requires EXACT equalities of the normalized traces of a realized pair (A,B) for r=1..k. What is actually proved, Proposition prop:momentmatch, delivers only approximate equality of EXPECTED traces (factor 1+-epsilon), and the paper admits it cannot match even expected traces exactly. No result in the paper converts approximate, in-expectation moment matching into quantile interlacing; 'Corollary applies in expectation' is not a valid mode of applying the corollary, and the paper itself cites jinmusco for the fact that approximate moment matching may fail to give pointwise CDF (hence quantile) closeness. The asserted end-to-end guarantee therefore exceeds what the formal content supports.

failure_location.quote: We prove the efficacy of this framework given certain bounds on the kernel function, and we provide empirical evidence for its accuracy.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Prove a new bridge theorem (e.g., high-probability near-matching of the traces of a realized B plus an approximate-moment-to-quantile bound), or weaken the advertised guarantee to what the cited tools support (Wasserstein-1 control via the muscomusco approach, or a purely heuristic method with empirical evidence).
issues.overall_effect: The central selling point - proved, subquadratic-time bounds on all eigenvalues / the k spectrum quantiles - is unestablished; dependent prose claims (the 'only subquadratic method to find bounds on the later eigenvalues', the intrinsic-dimension application) inherit the gap. The formal results themselves are not invalidated by this issue.

issues.why_classification: Every supported resolution either requires essentially new proof architecture (concentration of traces plus an approximate-moment-to-quantile theorem, which the paper itself flags as potentially requiring 'prohibitively close tolerances') or abandons/changes the central guarantee type from a pointwise quantile sandwich to a Wasserstein or purely empirical one; no comparable version of the advertised claim is currently established.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: which we may compute in $O(k^2)$ time \cite{golubvanloan}
In particular, it requires $O(mk^2)$ steps, where $m$ is the number of times we form $B$.

issues.failure_explanation: Each of the m trials forms a dense k-by-k kernel matrix B and computes all k of its eigenvalues. Forming B costs O(k^2) kernel evaluations, but computing the full spectrum of a general symmetric k-by-k matrix costs Theta(k^3) - the standard algorithms in the cited reference Golub-Van Loan are cubic. Hence the framework costs O(mk^3) in total, not the O(mk^2) asserted three times.

issues.failure_explanation: The hypothesis matches only the first k moments. The first k moments of the uniform distribution on the k-point set T determine T (hence all nu_i), but they do not determine the higher moments mu_i (i > k) of the n-point set S, so 'and therefore for each i in N' is false in general. The inference is load-bearing: the orthogonality transfer to T (eq:kroneckerprop) involves degrees up to i+j <= 2k, and the key claim (1) that the b_i are precisely the roots of P_k requires mu_0..mu_{2k-1} to equal the corresponding averages over T, since the coefficients of P_k are built from those moments. In general the roots of P_k are the Gauss quadrature nodes of S's own moment sequence, not the b_i, so claims (1) and (2) - and hence the reduction to the cited Christoffel-function CDF bounds - are unsupported under the stated hypothesis.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: for all $s\in[t,1]$.

issues.failure_explanation: As an exact equality demanded for all s in [t,1], the condition is unsatisfiable: at s=1 the ratio equals 1, forcing epsilon=0 (already the trivial one-vertex walks give ratio exactly s for normalized kernels, forcing epsilon=0), and ratio = s exactly for every walk pattern holds only in the Dirac limit, not for any positive-definite function - so the proposition is vacuous as stated, and the claim that some length scale lambda makes a Gaussian 'satisfy' it does not follow from the mere limit statement lim_{lambda->infty} ratio = s. Moreover, even taken formally the additive form s+epsilon cannot prove the two-sided conclusion: the lower bound uses s+epsilon >= (1-epsilon)s (true), but the upper bound needs ratio <= (1+epsilon)s, and s+epsilon <= (1+epsilon)s holds only when s >= 1, so the 'similar way' second inequality fails on [t,1). What the proof actually uses, and what the numerical examples support, is the relative two-sided condition ratio in [(1-epsilon)s, (1+epsilon)s].
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate eq:quickdecay as the relative two-sided condition (1-epsilon)s <= ratio <= (1+epsilon)s for s in [t,1] (with the product running to r), and prove satisfiability for peaky kernels, e.g., by upgrading the stated Gaussian limit to one uniform over s in [t,1] and over the finitely many walk patterns of length at most k.
issues.overall_effect: The paper's main trace-matching proposition is vacuous as stated, its upper-bound argument is invalid under the stated hypothesis, and no kernel is verified to satisfy the hypothesis; all numerical examples and the framework narrative rest on this proposition.
issues.title: Kernel decay hypothesis eq:quickdecay is unsatisfiable as stated and cannot yield the two-sided bound
issues.why_classification: A comparable proposition survives - the same conclusion under the corrected, plausibly satisfiable hypothesis - but the repair requires restating the central hypothesis and supplying a uniformity/existence argument the source does not contain; this is contained within the one result but is more than a local correction.

issues.failure_explanation: The source correctly computes the normalized moment as (n-k)!(k-l-1)!/(n-l-1)!, but the displayed Beta integral with (1-x)^{k-l} equals (n-k)!(k-l)!/(n-l)!, which differs from the claimed value by the factor (n-l)/(k-l) (e.g., n=4, k=2, l=0: the integral gives 1/6 while the moment is 1/3); the correct exponent is (1-x)^{k-l-1}. Consequently the Gram-matrix identifications are false as written: the v-family identity carries the wrong exponent, and the w-family identity computes the normalized mu_l, not mu_{l+1} as claimed. (Additionally, for n=k the measure x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^{k+1} is not finite and the functions leave V, although that case is trivially solvable with Z=1 a.s.) The conclusion survives: the same Gram argument with the corrected families (1-x)^{-(i+1)} for H_{k,n} and (1-x)^{-(i+3/2)} for H'_{k,n}, both linearly independent in V, shows both Hankel matrices are positive definite.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct the exponent in the Beta integral to (1-x)^{k-l-1} and re-derive the Gram representations with the shifted function families; optionally treat the degenerate case n=k separately.
